title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
content: An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class. As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen. The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter. The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school. Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class. "To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday. Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said. Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition. Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives. He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed". He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there. A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said. Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear. Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect. But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action. The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside. Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him. In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition". The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy". US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero". Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention. "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said. Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well". Kayla Epstein contributed to this report. The judge in the case said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness. The White House is facing growing adversity, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher, weeks before crucial midterm elections. The White House says the new press secretary is "transitioning out" of the role just days after taking the job. As the 3 November election approaches and both parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
content: Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades. Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too. So what is happening? Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale. And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east. The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living. Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers. Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons. Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony. Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation. A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too. Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign. The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead. The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder. One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue. The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president. They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night. But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands. The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership. Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement. Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard." Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth." An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward. After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system. Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos. "All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday. The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward". Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama. But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance. So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it. On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved. Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU. Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday. "These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence." Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being. The UK government has urged visitors to check media for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities. Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path. Flamingos have become a national symbol of protest, triggered by opposition to a luxury development. Protesters are angry after a man was allegedly killed by police for breaking a coronavirus curfew. title: Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
content: A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country. The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday. Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other". Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented. Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country. Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg. A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre. The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women. The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water. "Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said. Gift Skhosana, one of those held at the facility, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika it was "common practice" for patients to be chained. "They chain us as punishment [and] when you gain entry," he said. Despite this, Skhosana, who was a drug user, said the facility helped him get clean and overcome his addiction. Another person, who was not named, said his experience with the facility left him needing help mentally. The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; £137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church. Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said. Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families. The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday. Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.
